action_criteria.expected_evidence: MoCA 21/30 with losses in trail-making, cube, clock, digit span, serial sevens, letter fluency and delayed recall (2/5, 4/5 with cueing); no confabulation
action_criteria.label: Perform a validated bedside cognitive assessment and record the per-domain profile and whether delayed recall improves with cueing
action_criteria.rationale: A three-year decline in a heavy drinker needs a validated instrument and a per-domain profile, looking for cue-responsive recall versus the storage amnesia with confabulation of Korsakoff syndrome.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Timed-up-and-go 16.8 s, SPPB 7/12, short-stepped wide-based gait with preserved arm swing, 26% dual-task decay, truncal instability and a mildly positive Romberg
action_criteria.label: Perform timed gait and balance testing and separate the components of the gait disorder
action_criteria.rationale: Two falls and an unsteady gait in a patient with small-vessel disease, cerebellar signs and a neuropathy: timed testing quantifies the falls risk and documents the higher-level gait disorder VASCOG lists as a supporting feature.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Trail Making B 4th, SDMT 6th and FAS 9th percentile with recognition preserved (42nd percentile) and no confabulation
action_criteria.label: Order formal multi-domain neuropsychological testing to settle the executive-versus-amnestic attribution and to document a baseline for follow-up
action_criteria.rationale: Formal testing separates an executive, processing-speed profile with preserved recognition from the dense storage amnesia of alcohol-related Korsakoff syndrome.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MCV 102.6 fL, GGT 118 U/L and ALT 46 U/L; B12 214 pg/mL and thiamine 82 nmol/L low-normal; TSH, folate, RPR and HIV normal; LDL 128 mg/dL, triglycerides 210 mg/dL, HbA1c 5.8%
action_criteria.label: Order the reversible-cause screen and the vascular-risk assays that will be treated (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate, HbA1c, lipid panel)
action_criteria.rationale: In a drinker the reversible contributors (B12, folate, thyroid, metabolic and liver tests) must be measured, and the untreated lipid and glycaemic risk quantified.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Fazekas 3 white matter hyperintensity, three lacunes and one deep thalamic microbleed, superior vermian atrophy, normal mamillary bodies and MTA grade 1
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI reported in STRIVE-2 terms (FLAIR with a Fazekas grade, lacunes, DWI, SWI for microbleeds) and read it for both a vascular and an alcohol-related process
action_criteria.rationale: Imaging is where the vascular attribution is made, and the same study shows or excludes the cerebellar and diencephalic changes of alcohol-related damage.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the whole syndrome to alcohol in a patient whose decline progressed while intake fell and whose blood pressure was never controlled.
Do not give glucose-containing fluids without thiamine cover in a patient with chronic alcohol use.
Do not prescribe benzodiazepines outside a managed withdrawal in a patient with this falls risk.
Do not treat an unconfirmed Korsakoff syndrome as established in the absence of confabulation and with normal mamillary bodies.
Do not start an antiplatelet for covert small-vessel disease alone [ESO_2021_SVD].
Do not omit the vascular risk-factor treatment because the alcohol history is prominent.
required_recommendations: Explain to Mr Greco and his brother that the decline is subcortical vascular dementia from long-standing uncontrolled hypertension, and that alcohol contributes to the cerebellar and neuropathic parts of the gait disorder but does not explain the cognitive decline, which progressed while drinking fell [VASCOG_2014].

Lower blood pressure gradually to below 130/80 mmHg (currently 164/94 mmHg on irregularly taken amlodipine 5 mg), with supervised once-daily dosing and orthostatic BP checked at each change given his falls [ESO_2021_SVD].
Support complete abstinence from alcohol through a specialist alcohol service, and continue oral thiamine.
Replace vitamin B12 or confirm deficiency with methylmalonic acid (B12 214 pg/mL with alcohol use, long-term pantoprazole and a sensory neuropathy), and review the need for pantoprazole.
Offer smoking-cessation treatment (current smoker, 30 pack-years) and a statin for his cardiovascular risk (LDL 128 mg/dL, untreated).
Address safety: an automatic gas shut-off or supervision after two episodes of leaving the gas on, his brother continuing to manage finances, and a falls and balance programme.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no diagnostic role in vascular cognitive impairment; the course is slowly progressive without fluctuation, and the single seizure six years ago was a provoked withdrawal seizure.

A presynaptic dopaminergic study answers the Lewy-body question, not the vascular one, and there is no spontaneous parkinsonism, no fluctuating cognition with hallucinations and no REM sleep behaviour disorder
No parkinsonism, fluctuation, hallucinations or dream enactment: cardiac sympathetic imaging is a Lewy-body test with no question to answer here.
A three-year progressive decline with untreated hypertension and past heavy drinking, not a subacute multidomain syndrome: a paraneoplastic or autoimmune-encephalitis battery has no indication.
MRI is available and not contraindicated; CT cannot show microbleeds, siderosis or small lacunes.
Lacunes and confluent white matter disease without any cortical or territorial infarct: a cardioembolic source would not explain the burden or change management.
Pure small-vessel disease with a regular pulse; prolonged rhythm monitoring changes neither the diagnosis nor the treatment.

accepted: Vascular dementia: subcortical ischaemic (small-vessel) type from untreated hypertension, with a coexisting alcohol-related cerebellar syndrome and sensory polyneuropathy contributing to the gait disorder
major neurocognitive disorder due to vascular disease

differential.key_features: Twenty-five years of heavy intake makes alcohol a contributor, but as the sole cause it is excluded: the decline progressed across a year of substantially reduced intake, there is no Korsakoff phenotype, and the Fazekas 3 burden with three lacunes is sufficient on its own
No ophthalmoparesis, no acute confusional episodes in the history, no confabulation, normal mamillary bodies and no periaqueductal signal change; thiamine is low-normal on supplementation
Cue-responsive recall, preserved hippocampi and an executive-predominant profile
No stigmata of chronic liver disease, no asterixis, albumin 3.9 g/dL and only mildly raised ALT; no clinical or biochemical evidence of hepatic decompensation
B12 214 pg/mL is low-normal and warrants correction, but cannot account for a Fazekas 3 burden with three lacunes

key_clinical_evidence: The temporal test is decisive: alcohol-related cognitive impairment stabilises or improves with reduced intake, so progression across a year of substantial reduction implicates a second, still-active process
Korsakoff syndrome has a positive phenotype — dense storage amnesia with confabulation and mamillary body atrophy — and its absence is informative rather than merely unproven
Two comorbid processes can each be identified on one MRI: a Fazekas 3 small-vessel burden and superior vermian cerebellar atrophy have different causes and different implications
Untreated hypertension in a patient whose drinking has fallen is the actionable driver, and adherence is the intervention
Attributing everything to alcohol is the failure mode this case is built around: it removes the treatable vascular diagnosis from view

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Moderate: two plausible attributions, resolved by the temporal relationship to reduced drinking, the absence of a Korsakoff phenotype and the severity of the vascular burden
key_educational_points: Progression during a period of reduced drinking is the argument that separates vascular from alcohol-related cognitive decline
Korsakoff syndrome should be diagnosed on its positive features, not assumed from a drinking history

A prominent alcohol history is the commonest reason a treatable vascular diagnosis is missed

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Fabio Greco is a 66-year-old former lorry driver who attends with his brother. He drank between 100 and 120 grams of ethanol daily for about twenty-five years and has cut down to around forty grams in the past year. Over three years his brother has watched him become slower, more forgetful and less able to organise: he cannot manage his own benefits paperwork, forgets to pay for things, and has twice left the flat with the gas on. He is unsteady, particularly in the dark, and has fallen twice. He also reports numbness in his feet going back several years. His brother is clear that the cognitive decline has continued during the past year in which drinking has fallen substantially, which is the observation that brought them to the clinic: they expected improvement and did not see it. He had a withdrawal seizure six years ago and two withdrawal episodes. He denies double vision, has never had an episode of confusion with unsteadiness and eye movement problems, and has never been admitted for encephalopathy. His blood pressure has been recorded above 160 systolic on most visits and he takes amlodipine irregularly. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuations and no dream enactment.
